questions.question: Explain what the space race was and why it was part of the Cold War.
questions.expected_answer: The space race (1957 to about 1975) was the US-Soviet competition to achieve firsts in space, from satellites to the Moon. It was part of the Cold War because launch rockets were developed from missiles (R-7; von Braun's V-2 work; Korolev), so space success showed the ability to strike with nuclear weapons; satellites could spy; and each success was propaganda for capitalism or communism, especially for newly independent countries. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty banned claims to the Moon and nuclear weapons in orbit.

questions.question: Describe the Soviet Union's early achievements in space and the American response.
questions.expected_answer: Sputnik 1 (4 October 1957; 84 kg, orbit about 96 minutes, about 15 a day) caused the Sputnik crisis; Sputnik 2 carried Laika (November 1957); Vanguard exploded (December 1957). The US launched Explorer 1 (31 January 1958), created NASA (1958) and funded science education. Soviet firsts continued: Luna 2 and 3 (1959), Gagarin first human in space (12 April 1961, 108 minutes), Tereshkova (1963), Leonov's spacewalk (1965). Shepard (May 1961) and Glenn (February 1962) followed. Kennedy (25 May 1961) set the Moon goal.

questions.question: Describe the Moon landing of 1969 and the consequences of the space race, including South Africa's role.
questions.expected_answer: After Gemini, the Apollo 1 fire and Apollo 8 (Earthrise, 1968), Apollo 11 launched on 16 July 1969; Armstrong and Aldrin landed on 20 July while Collins orbited; about 600 million watched; twelve astronauts landed by 1972. Consequences: US propaganda victory; cost about 25 billion dollars, criticised by civil rights leaders; satellites for weather, communications and GPS; cooperation (Apollo-Soyuz 1975, ISS from 1998). NASA's Hartebeesthoek station (1961) tracked missions until 1975; today MeerKAT, SANSA (2010); Shuttleworth first African in space (2002).
